name: basex
desc: Light-weight XML database and XPath/XQuery processor
why: A lightweight XML database with XQuery, a rarely-touched corner of data processing with a real old-school flavour.

brief.what_it_is: BaseX is an open source XML database engine and XQuery processor, written in Java. It stores and queries large collections of XML, HTML, JSON, CSV and other textual resources, plus binary resources. You can run XQuery expressions from the command line without entering the console, or use its desktop or web-based GUI, which the docs describe as an IDE with visualizations for exploring data. It also supports RESTXQ, which lets you build web applications in XQuery.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents BaseX as a robust, high-performance XML database and a highly compliant XQuery processor, and as a framework for data-intensive web applications. Its tagline is "Lightweight and High-Performance Data Processing".
brief.how_it_works: The README describes four entry points in the basex-core package under org.basex: BaseX (console mode), BaseXServer (a server instance that waits for requests), BaseXClient (console mode that talks to the server), and BaseXGUI (graphical interface). The docs describe a client/server architecture and a storage layer, but I did not read those sections in detail.

commands_seen.context: From the GitHub README: 'try `-h` to list the available command line options'. It is a flag, not a full command line, and the README does not show it being run with a specific executable.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a Download BaseX 12.4 button. The GitHub README is aimed at building from source and says JDK 21 and JUnit are required to compile the complete sources, with Eclipse as the default IDE. I did not check what the Homebrew formula pulls in, so I cannot confirm whether a separate Java runtime is needed for the brew install. Nothing in the pages I read covers accounts or first-run configuration.
brief.standout: Few XML databases ship a full XQuery 4.0 processor with the W3C Update and Full-Text extensions, plus RESTXQ and a GUI with data visualizations, in one lightweight package. The docs also link to BXFiddle, an online place to run queries without installing anything.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists releases BaseX 12.2 (2026-01-20), 12.3 (2026-04-16) and 12.4 (2026-05-28). The docs describe BaseX 12 as the current release, with BaseX 11 still available and a BaseX 13 snapshot. I did not see a last commit date.
brief.caveats: Building from source needs JDK 21 and JUnit, and the README points to Eclipse as the default IDE. The docs call BaseX platform-independent and BSD-licensed, but I did not check the license file. The homepage tagline says it runs out of the box, but I did not verify that claim.
quotes: BaseX is lightweight, easy to install, and runs out of the box…
BaseX is platform-independent and BSD-licensed (see Wikipedia for more information).

https://github.com/BaseXdb/basex — worked; README with build and class overview, not on the homepage but used to fill commands and install notes

judge.reason: BaseX makes XML a queryable database with a full XQuery processor and RESTXQ, opening a genuinely unusual alternative to SQL-centric data tools.

entry.title: BaseX
entry.tldr: A lightweight XML database and XQuery processor that lets you query XML, JSON and CSV with a functional query language most developers never meet.
entry.deeper_look:
BaseX is a database engine written in Java for storing and querying collections of XML, HTML, JSON, CSV and other text, plus binary resources. You can run XQuery expressions straight from the command line, use a console, or open a desktop GUI that the docs describe as an IDE with visualizations for exploring data.

The idea underneath it is XQuery, a query language built for tree-shaped documents rather than tables. Where SQL asks questions of rows, XQuery walks and reshapes nested structures, and it is a full functional language rather than only a way to filter. BaseX describes itself as a highly compliant processor, with XQuery 4.0 and the W3C Update and Full-Text extensions.

The README lists four entry points: a console, a server that waits for requests, a client that talks to that server, and the GUI. That maps to the executables brew installs, including `basexserver`, `basexclient` and `basexhttp`. BaseX also supports RESTXQ, which lets you build web applications in XQuery itself.

The project's tagline is "Lightweight and High-Performance Data Processing". It is a door into a corner of data processing that is old, well specified and still maintained.
entry.install:
brew install basex
# Java is required; the formula lists openjdk as a dependency

try_this.what_happens: Lists the available command line options, as the README suggests.
Opens the desktop GUI, where you can write queries and explore data visually.
Starts a database server that waits for requests from clients such as basexclient.

entry.whats_unique: Few XML databases ship an XQuery 4.0 processor with the Update and Full-Text extensions, RESTXQ and a visual GUI in one lightweight package.
entry.caveats: The brief did not check what the brew install pulls in or how first run behaves, and the docs are the best place to learn XQuery itself.
